props.title: The Assassination of Jesse James by the Coward Robert Ford
props.initialSlug: The Betrayal That Shook the West

sections.content: The Assassination of Jesse James by the Coward Robert Ford (2007) revolutionized the modern Western through Roger Deakins' haunting cinematography and Andrew Dominik's patient, poetic direction. Like Days of Heaven (1978), it treats the American frontier as a dreamlike canvas, using natural light and wide shots to create an almost mythological atmosphere. Brad Pitt's Jesse James emerges as a paranoid, violent man grappling with his own legend, while Casey Affleck's Robert Ford delivers a masterclass in repressed obsession. The film's deliberate pacing and 160-minute runtime allow it to explore celebrity worship and American mythmaking with unprecedented depth.

sections.content: The film's influence on subsequent Westerns can't be overstated. True Grit (2010) and Slow West (2015) adopted similar contemplative approaches, while The Power of the Dog (2021) echoed its psychological complexity. Dominik's film marked a decisive shift away from action-driven Westerns toward character studies that use the genre to explore deeper themes of American identity, fame, and violence.

The film's treatment of celebrity culture feels remarkably prescient. Like Network (1976) and A Face in the Crowd (1957), it examines the dark side of fame and public adoration. Ford's tragic obsession with James parallels modern fan culture, while James's awareness of his own myth anticipates our current discourse about celebrity and media manipulation. SUBHEAD: Deconstructing the American Myth

sections.content: The film's visual approach revolutionized period filmmaking. Deakins' cinematography, particularly his use of natural light and shallow focus, influenced films like The Revenant (2015) and 1917 (2019). The narration technique, combining omniscient commentary with intimate character moments, created a new template for historical dramas, evident in later works like The Grand Budapest Hotel (2014).
